name: Cyclic Sighing (Physiological Sigh Pattern)
purpose: Rapidly reduce acute arousal and improve mood via exhale-emphasized double inhale + long exhale.
problem: Acute stress, elevated respiratory rate, low positive affect, need for a brief downshift.
minimum: 1–3 sighs (~30–60 seconds) for acute relief; 5 minutes for studied daily dose
steps: Sit or stand comfortably with upright posture.
Inhale slowly through the nose until lungs feel mostly full.
Without exhaling, take a second shorter inhale through the nose to maximally inflate the lungs.
Exhale slowly and fully through the mouth (or nose) until lungs empty.
Repeat continuously for ~5 minutes (or 1–3 cycles for acute use).
Return to normal breathing; notice body sensations without forcing calm.
when: Acute stress spikes, pre-meeting nerves, end-of-day wind-down, or as a daily 5-min mood practice.
short: Often reduced respiratory rate and improved positive affect within minutes to days of practice.
long: In a 28-day RCT, daily cyclic sighing improved mood more than matched mindfulness and reduced resting respiratory rate.
mechanism: Double inhale recruits collapsed alveoli (physiological sigh); prolonged exhale increases parasympathetic influence via pulmonary stretch and vagal pathways; reduced chemoreflex drive may lower respiratory rate over time.
research: Yilmaz Balban et al., Cell Reports Medicine 2023 (NCT05304000): remote RCT, daily 5-min cyclic sighing vs box breathing, cyclic hyperventilation, mindfulness; cyclic sighing best for positive affect and respiratory-rate reduction. PubMed 36630953; DOI 10.1016/j.xcrm.2022.100895. Note: HR/HRV did not significantly differ; healthy adults; remote delivery.
risks: Lightheadedness if overdone; mouth-breathing dryness; may feel unusual initially.
avoid: Modify if severe respiratory disease, recent thoracic surgery, uncontrolled panic with breath-focus intolerance, or pregnancy-related breathing limits—use gentle single long exhales instead of forced maximal fills.
creator: Studied by Yilmaz Balban, Huberman, Spiegel et al. (Stanford); pattern based on known physiological sighing (respiratory neuroscience).

name: Box Breathing (Square Breathing)
purpose: Stabilize attention and arousal with equal inhale–hold–exhale–hold timing.
problem: Performance anxiety, scattered attention, need for structured paced breathing under pressure.
steps: Choose a count you can sustain without strain (commonly 4 seconds each side; some use 3–5).
Inhale through the nose for the count.
Hold lungs gently full for the same count (no straining).
Exhale through nose or mouth for the same count.
Hold empty (or near-empty) for the same count.
Repeat for 2–5 minutes; stop if dizzy.
when: Pre-performance, between tasks, tactical stress contexts, brief reset.
short: Subjective calm and attentional anchoring; may reduce state anxiety for some users.
long: In Balban 2023, box breathing improved mood/anxiety similarly to other groups but was not superior to cyclic sighing on primary mood/respiratory outcomes.
mechanism: Paced breathing + mild breath holds provide cognitive structure (attentional load) and may modulate autonomic balance; equal counts are a convenience heuristic, not an individually optimized resonance rate.
research: Comparator arm in Yilmaz Balban et al. 2023 (Cell Rep Med). Broader paced-breathing literature supports slow breathing for HRV/stress more than the specific equal-hold box pattern. Limited high-quality trials isolating box breathing alone.
risks: Breath holds can raise CO2/discomfort; dizziness; hypervigilance if counts are too long.
avoid: Avoid long holds if pregnancy, uncontrolled hypertension, panic disorder with breath-hold sensitivity, COPD/severe asthma. Shorten or remove holds.
sources: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36630953/ ; Fincham et al. Sci Rep 2023 https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-022-27247-y
creator: Popularized in tactical/performance settings (often linked to Navy SEAL training popularization; exact single inventor unclear).

name: Coherent / Resonance Frequency Breathing (~6 breaths/min)
purpose: Maximize respiratory sinus arrhythmia / HRV via slow paced breathing near ~0.1 Hz.
problem: Chronic stress load, low HRV, need for a trainable autonomic downshift practice.
steps: Sit upright, relaxed shoulders; breathe through the nose if comfortable.
Pace at about 6 breaths per minute (e.g., ~5 s inhale, ~5 s exhale) OR find personal resonance (~4.5–7/min) if using HRV guidance.
Prefer slightly longer exhale than inhale if that feels easier (common coaching cue).
Breathe gently—avoid overbreathing; if lightheaded, reduce depth.
Optional: visual/audio pacer; optional HRV biofeedback to maximize LF/RSA amplitude.
Practice daily; Lehrer protocols historically used ~20 min twice daily with biofeedback.
when: Daily stress regulation, pre-sleep wind-down (if not too alerting), HRV training blocks, anxiety adjunct.
short: Increased HRV/RSA during practice; often calmer mood and lower perceived stress.
long: HRV biofeedback / resonance breathing associated with small–moderate benefits for stress, some anxiety/depression, and BP in reviews; individual resonance may help but fixed ~6/min is often sufficient.
mechanism: Near ~0.1 Hz, respiration, heart-rate oscillations, and baroreflex resonate, maximizing RSA and stimulating baroreflex gain (Lehrer/Vaschillo model).
research: Lehrer & Gevirtz Frontiers Psychol 2014 PMC4104929; Steffen et al. 2017 resonance breathing HRV/BP/mood PMC5575449; Frontiers Neurosci 2020 practical guide to RF assessment. Newer work questions necessity of exact individual RF vs fixed 6/min.
risks: Overbreathing (low CO2) causing dizziness/tingling; frustration with pacing; rare anxiety increase with interoceptive focus.
avoid: Severe respiratory disease; acute panic if breath focus worsens symptoms—use shorter sessions or therapist guidance. Capnometry advised in clinical HRVB when available.
creator: Paul Lehrer, Evgeny Vaschillo, and collaborators (HRV biofeedback / resonance frequency training).

name: Diaphragmatic (Belly) Breathing
purpose: Reduce accessory-muscle breathing and promote slower, deeper abdominal expansion for relaxation.
problem: Chest-dominant breathing under stress, somatic anxiety, tension.
steps: Lie down or sit; one hand on chest, one on abdomen.
Inhale slowly through nose so the abdomen rises more than the chest.
Exhale slowly through nose or pursed lips, abdomen falling.
Keep shoulders relaxed; do not force maximal depth.
Continue 5–15 minutes; optionally combine with 6/min pacing.
when: General anxiety reduction; physiotherapy adjunct for dysfunctional breathing; wind-down.
short: Reduced muscle tension and subjective anxiety for many practitioners.
long: RCTs and reviews support diaphragmatic/slow breathing for anxiety symptoms with small–moderate effects; quality and protocols vary.
mechanism: Reduced accessory muscle use, increased tidal volume at lower rate, possible vagal/parasympathetic facilitation, interoceptive attention shift.
research: Diaphragmatic breathing RCTs for anxiety (e.g., Chen et al. related work); Fincham et al. 2023 breathwork meta-analysis (Sci Rep) small–moderate stress effects; technique heterogeneity is a limitation.
risks: Hyperventilation if too deep/fast; abdominal discomfort; increased awareness of breath may worsen panic in some.
avoid: Acute abdominal pain/surgery; severe COPD may need clinician-guided breathing rehab rather than DIY max belly breathing.
creator: Longstanding clinical/physiotherapy practice; not a single inventor.

name: 4-7-8 Breathing (as popularized by Weil)
purpose: Use a counted inhale–hold–long-exhale pattern as a bedtime or acute calming cue.
problem: Difficulty falling asleep, acute anxiety, need for a simple memorable ratio.
typical: 4 breath cycles (~1–2 minutes); repeat up to ~8 cycles if needed
steps: Place tongue tip behind upper front teeth (Weil cue; optional).
Exhale fully through mouth with a whoosh sound.
Close mouth; inhale quietly through nose for count of 4.
Hold breath for count of 7.
Exhale completely through mouth for count of 8.
Repeat for 4 cycles initially; do not exceed ~8 cycles when new.
when: In bed when sleep onset is delayed; acute anxiety if holds are tolerated.
short: May feel calmer via extended exhale and attentional focus; acute autonomic changes in some small studies.
long: Limited high-quality evidence specific to the exact 4-7-8 ratio; benefits likely overlap with slow breathing + prolonged exhale. Not a validated insomnia monotherapy.
mechanism: Proposed: extended exhale and mild hypercapnia during hold; attentional distraction from rumination. Specific 4:7:8 timing is largely a mnemonic.
research: Sparse dedicated RCTs for Weil exact protocol; related paced/exhale-focused breathing has better support (Balban 2023; Lehrer HRVB). Small 4-7-8 studies show autonomic/anxiety changes—interpret cautiously.
risks: Breath holds can cause discomfort, dizziness, or panic in sensitive people.
avoid: Skip or shorten holds in pregnancy, uncontrolled hypertension, panic with breath-hold aversion, or respiratory disease. Prefer cyclic sighing or 6/min breathing without holds.
sources: Andrew Weil public educational materials (popularization); compare Balban 2023 and Lehrer HRVB literature.
creator: Popularized by Andrew Weil, MD (pranayama-inspired counted breathing).

name: Alternate Nostril Breathing (Nadi Shodhana / Anulom Vilom)
purpose: Traditional paced unilateral nostril breathing used for calm focus.
problem: Restlessness, desire for a structured traditional breathing ritual.
steps: Sit upright. Thumb closes right nostril, ring finger closes left (classic; adaptations OK).
Close right; inhale left.
Close left; open right; exhale right.
Inhale right; switch; exhale left.
Continue 5–10 minutes at comfortable pace.
Optional equal counts; advanced retentions only with teacher guidance.
when: Transition into meditation/focus work; evening downshift if calming.
short: Often subjective calm and focused attention; some small studies show autonomic/HRV changes.
long: Evidence preliminary/mixed; many studies small or high bias risk. Treat as traditional with plausible paced-breathing benefits.
mechanism: Traditional: balance of ida/pingala (not scientific). Scientific candidates: paced breathing effects, attentional control, mild unilateral nasal airflow differences (limited evidence).
research: Small trials and yoga research reviews report anxiety/HRV changes; quality generally lower than Western paced-breathing RCTs.
risks: Finger pressure discomfort; nasal congestion frustration; advanced breath holds add risk.
avoid: Significant nasal obstruction, active sinus infection, or breath-hold variants if contraindicated.
sources: Traditional hatha yoga texts; modern small clinical/yoga studies (heterogeneous).
creator: Classical yoga tradition (hatha/pranayama lineages).

name: Exhale-Emphasized Paced Breathing (No Holds)
purpose: Simple calm breathing without holds: longer exhale than inhale.
problem: Need easy breathing tool when box holds or 4-7-8 holds are poorly tolerated.
steps: Inhale nose ~3–4 seconds.
Exhale nose/mouth ~5–7 seconds.
No forced holds.
Keep breaths gentle.
Continue 5 minutes.
when: Anxiety with hold intolerance; bridge to resonance breathing.
short: Calm via extended exhale.
long: Consistent with Balban finding favoring exhale emphasis vs matched mindfulness.
mechanism: Extended exhale / pulmonary stretch → parasympathetic bias hypotheses.
research: Aligned with cyclic sighing emphasis (Balban 2023) and slow-breathing literature.
risks: Minimal if gentle.
avoid: Severe respiratory disease—physiotherapist guidance.
creator: Applied synthesis from paced-breathing research.

name: Cyclic Hyperventilation with Retention (Caution Protocol)
purpose: Inhale-emphasized cycling with short exhales and retention (studied comparator; not first-line calm tool).
problem: Sometimes sought for alertness/activation; used in some breathwork traditions.
minimum: Not recommended as default self-help for stress—prefer cyclic sighing.
steps: Only if medically appropriate and not seeking calm: relatively vigorous inhales with shorter passive exhales for cycles, with brief retention as instructed.
Stop immediately if dizziness, tingling, chest pain, or panic.
Prefer cyclic sighing / resonance breathing for stress/anxiety.
when: Research context or carefully supervised activation—not for panic, insomnia, or hypertension.
short: May increase arousal; in Balban 2023 still reduced anxiety vs baseline but was not best mood protocol.
long: Not superior to cyclic sighing for mood; hyperventilation-style practices carry more physiological risk.
mechanism: Lowered CO2 (hypocapnia) alters cerebral blood flow; can create lightheadedness/tingling; retention adds CO2 rebound.
research: Comparator arm in Yilmaz Balban et al. 2023. Distinct from Wim Hof Method (separate evidence/risks).
risks: Syncope, arrhythmia risk in susceptible people, panic, hypocapnia; never practice in water or while driving.
avoid: Cardiovascular disease, pregnancy, epilepsy, fainting history, bipolar mania risk, panic disorder—avoid. Not for children.
creator: Operationalized in Balban/Huberman trial; related to cyclic hyperventilation traditions.

name: Progressive Muscle Relaxation (PMR)
purpose: Systematically tense and release muscle groups to reduce somatic tension and anxiety.
problem: Muscle tension, somatic anxiety, sleep-onset difficulty related to bodily arousal.
steps: Sit or lie down in a quiet place.
For each muscle group: tense gently 5–7 seconds, then release 20–30 seconds, noticing contrast.
Common order: hands/forearms → upper arms → forehead → eyes/cheeks → jaw → neck → shoulders → chest → abdomen → thighs → calves → feet.
Use only mild–moderate tension—never pain.
End with brief whole-body scan of residual tension.
when: Evening wind-down, acute somatic anxiety, insomnia behavioral component (relaxation training).
short: Reduced muscle tension and state anxiety for many users.
long: Meta-analyses support relaxation training including PMR for anxiety with moderate effects; AASM lists relaxation among behavioral insomnia options. Component network meta-analysis suggests relaxation alone may be less critical than sleep restriction/stimulus control for insomnia remission.
mechanism: Learned discrimination of tension vs relaxation; reduced sympathetic/somatic arousal; attentional shift from worry to body sensations.
research: Manzoni et al. BMC Psychiatry 2008 relaxation meta-analysis PMC2427027; Muhammad Khir et al. 2024 PMR systematic review PMC10844009; AASM 2021 behavioral insomnia guidelines.
risks: Muscle strain if over-tensing; paradoxical anxiety; trauma survivors may find body focus activating.
avoid: Acute injuries; uncontrolled hypertension for strong isometric holds (use passive PMR); psychosis; severe trauma without support.
creator: Edmund Jacobson (Progressive Relaxation).

name: Autogenic Training (AT)
purpose: Self-generated passive concentration on heaviness/warmth and calm bodily states.
problem: Chronic tension, anxiety, psychosomatic stress symptoms.
typical: 10–20 minutes per session; traditionally trained over weeks
steps: Sit or lie comfortably; eyes closed.
Silently repeat standard formulas with passive attention (e.g., My arms are heavy; My arms are warm; calm heartbeat/breathing; solar plexus warmth; forehead cool).
Do not force sensations; observe passively.
Practice regularly; traditionally learned with instructor for full protocol.
when: Daily self-regulation; anxiety adjunct; some clinical AT programs.
short: Warmth/heaviness sensations and subjective calm when training succeeds.
long: Systematic reviews suggest benefits for stress/anxiety; some meta-analytic estimates large but based on limited/heterogeneous trials—grade moderate-to-preliminary for general use.
mechanism: Self-hypnosis-like passive concentration; learned autonomic self-regulation; expectancy and attentional control.
research: Seo & Kim 2019 AT stress meta-analysis PubMed 31477667; earlier AT reviews (Stetter & Kupper).
risks: Anxiety increase in some; rare dissociation; not a substitute for medical care of somatic symptoms.
avoid: Acute psychosis; severe depression with passive suicidal ideation without care; trauma triggers with passive body focus.
creator: Johannes Heinrich Schultz (1930s).

name: Body Scan (MBSR Element)
purpose: Systematically move attention through the body with nonjudgmental awareness.
problem: Mind wandering, tension unawareness, need for mindfulness anchor.
steps: Lie down or sit; close eyes if comfortable.
Begin at feet (or head); notice sensations without trying to change them.
Move slowly region by region.
When mind wanders, note gently and return.
End with whole-body awareness for a few breaths.
when: Mindfulness practice, wind-down, stress reduction programs.
short: Increased body awareness; often mild relaxation; sometimes sleepiness.
long: MBSR as a package has moderate evidence for stress/anxiety/depression symptoms vs waitlist; isolated body-scan evidence thinner than full program.
mechanism: Interoceptive attention training; decentering from rumination; possible autonomic calming secondary to sustained attention.
research: MBSR evidence base (Kabat-Zinn); mindfulness meta-analyses for anxiety/depression. Attribute stronger evidence to MBSR package than stand-alone scan.
risks: Trauma reactivation; frustration; sleepiness when driving after.
avoid: Active PTSD without trauma-sensitive guidance; acute mania; if lying down triggers panic—sit upright.
sources: Kabat-Zinn MBSR curriculum; mindfulness clinical trial literature.
creator: Jon Kabat-Zinn (MBSR formalization); vipassana-derived roots.

name: Yoga Nidra / NSDR (Non-Sleep Deep Rest)
purpose: Guided rest inducing deep relaxation while typically remaining behaviorally awake; rest-without-requiring-sleep framing.
problem: High stress, recovery need when sleep is insufficient, structured rest; adjunct for insomnia symptoms (not proven sleep replacement).
minimum: 10 minutes guided body awareness + breath rest
steps: Lie down in a quiet safe place; use headphones with a reputable guided script.
Set intention/resolve if script includes sankalpa (optional traditional element).
Follow rotation of consciousness through body, breath, imagery as guided.
Remain still; falling asleep is OK—not a failure.
After ending cue, reorient slowly before standing.
Do NOT claim or expect this to replace nocturnal sleep physiological functions.
when: Afternoon recovery, evening wind-down, high cognitive load days, insomnia adjunct under guidance.
short: Reduced subjective stress/arousal; sometimes local EEG slow-wave features while scored awake; respiratory rate may fall.
long: Preliminary evidence for improved subjective sleep and some PSG metrics in small trials; mixed lab findings vs quiet rest. Promising but not equivalent to CBT-I or replacing sleep debt.
mechanism: Guided attention + reduced sensory load may produce deep relaxation and local-sleep-like EEG features without whole-organism sleep. Traditional: yogic conscious sleep. Scientific claim of replacing sleep is not strongly supported.
research: Datta et al. NMJI 2021 (YN vs CBT-I, small RCT); local sleep EEG PMC9315270; PLOS One 2023 cognition/sleep novices; 2023 sleep-lab feasibility mixed vs quiet rest; EEG systematic reviews heterogeneous.
risks: Dissociation; falling asleep in unsafe contexts; delaying medical insomnia care.
avoid: Narcolepsy diagnostic confusion; untreated severe OSA; trauma-sensitive needs—choose secular scripts. Not a substitute for prescribed sleep therapy.
creator: Modern Yoga Nidra systematized by Swami Satyananda Saraswati et al.; NSDR popularized by Andrew Huberman as umbrella label.

name: Stimulus Control Therapy (CBT-I Component)
purpose: Re-associate bed/bedroom with sleep by eliminating incompatible bed behaviors and regulating sleep–wake contingencies.
problem: Chronic insomnia with conditioned arousal in bed (clock-watching, worry in bed).
typical: Ongoing nightly rules (behavioral regimen), not a timed exercise
minimum: Consistent application for ≥1–2 weeks to evaluate
steps: Use bed/bedroom only for sleep and sex (no work, scrolling, TV).
Go to bed only when sleepy.
If unable to sleep after ~15–20 minutes (rough estimate, avoid obsessive clock-watching), leave bed; do quiet non-stimulating activity in dim light; return when sleepy.
Repeat as needed.
Keep a fixed wake time every day including weekends.
Avoid daytime napping (or keep very brief/early if needed).
when: Chronic insomnia disorder—ideally within full CBT-I under clinician guidance.
short: May increase temporary sleepiness/frustration early while extinguishing conditioned arousal.
long: AASM supports stimulus control; 2024 component network meta-analysis finds stimulus control contributes to sleep quality/continuity improvements.
mechanism: Classical/operant conditioning: extinguish bed–wake association; strengthen bed–sleep association; consolidate sleep drive with fixed wake time.
research: AASM 2021 CPG for behavioral/psychological insomnia treatments PMC7853203; Edinger et al. systematic review; Furukawa et al. JAMA Psychiatry 2024 component network meta-analysis.
risks: Temporary sleep loss; safety if drowsy driving; partner disruption.
avoid: Clinician guidance if bipolar spectrum (sleep loss mania risk), seizure disorders, high-risk occupations, pregnancy with medical complexity. Clinical protocol—not casual biohacking.
creator: Richard Bootzin (stimulus control therapy for insomnia).

name: Sleep Restriction Therapy (CBT-I Component)
purpose: Temporarily limit time in bed to match average sleep time, consolidating sleep, then titrate upward.
problem: Chronic insomnia with low sleep efficiency (long time in bed, fragmented sleep).
minimum: Requires baseline sleep diary ≥1 week before starting
steps: Track sleep diary (time in bed, estimated total sleep).
Set time-in-bed window ≈ average total sleep time (often with a floor, e.g., ≥5–5.5 h—clinician sets).
Fix wake time; derive bedtime from window.
No additional time in bed outside window.
When sleep efficiency improves (often ≥85–90% for a week), extend time in bed by ~15–20 minutes.
Continue titration until optimal consolidation with adequate duration.
when: Chronic insomnia—strongly prefer trained CBT-I clinician.
short: Increased sleepiness, irritability, cognitive slowing early—expected and monitored.
long: Among the most potent CBT-I components for sleep continuity/efficiency (network meta-analysis).
mechanism: Increases homeostatic sleep pressure; reduces excess time awake in bed; consolidates sleep.
research: AASM 2021 guideline; Furukawa et al. JAMA Psychiatry 2024 cNMA—sleep restriction among critical components. ACP CBT-I guideline context.
risks: Significant daytime impairment; drowsy driving; mania precipitation; seizure risk in predisposed.
avoid: High-risk jobs, bipolar/mania predisposition, uncontrolled epilepsy, untreated severe OSA without guidance, pregnancy—clinician decision. Do not DIY aggressively.
creator: Arthur Spielman (sleep restriction therapy).

name: Behavioral Wind-Down Routine
purpose: Create a consistent pre-sleep buffer that reduces cognitive/physiological arousal.
problem: Sleep onset delay from evening stimulation, work spillover, bright light/screens.
steps: Set a nightly off-ramp alarm 30–60 min before target bedtime.
Dim lights; prefer warm/low lux lighting.
Stop work email and activating content; switch to low-arousal activities (reading, light stretching, PMR, slow breathing).
Avoid clock obsession; keep bedroom cool and dark for sleep.
If using CBT-I, ensure wind-down does not become long lying awake in bed (combine with stimulus control).
when: Habitual delayed sleep onset; high evening cognitive load.
short: Lower pre-sleep arousal; easier sleep initiation for many.
long: Supports sleep hygiene + CBT-I context; sleep hygiene alone is weak as monotherapy (AASM).
mechanism: Reduced sensory/cognitive stimulation; circadian-friendly light; conditioned relaxation cues.
research: Sleep hygiene alone insufficient per AASM; wind-down practically useful within multicomponent care.
risks: Becoming another performance demand.
avoid: If wind-down becomes lengthy wakefulness in bed, apply stimulus control instead.
creator: Clinical sleep medicine / CBT-I practice synthesis.

name: Caffeine Timing Cutoff
purpose: Reduce caffeine-related sleep disruption by stopping intake sufficiently before bedtime.
problem: Sleep latency/continuity problems with afternoon/evening caffeine.
typical: Policy: no caffeine within 8–10+ hours of bedtime (individualize)
minimum: Avoid caffeine after early afternoon if sensitive
steps: Estimate bedtime; set last-caffeine time (common heuristic 8–10 hours prior; half-life ~5 h average, wide variability).
Include hidden sources (tea, cola, chocolate, pre-workout, some analgesics).
Trial 1–2 weeks; track sleep diary.
If still impaired, move cutoff earlier or reduce total daily dose.
when: Insomnia or non-restorative sleep with regular caffeine use.
short: May improve sleep onset/continuity within days for sensitive individuals.
long: Pharmacokinetic rationale strong; experimental support that evening caffeine impairs sleep—individual differences large.
mechanism: Adenosine receptor antagonism maintains wakefulness; residual caffeine can delay sleep and reduce quality.
research: Laboratory caffeine–sleep studies; clinical sleep education summaries. Not a cure for chronic insomnia disorder alone.
risks: Withdrawal headache/fatigue if abrupt large cuts—taper if heavy user.
avoid: Not applicable as sole therapy for severe insomnia; consider medical causes.
sources: Peer-reviewed caffeine–sleep experimental literature; clinical sleep guidance.
creator: N/A (pharmacology-informed behavioral rule).

name: Morning Outdoor Light Timing
purpose: Anchor circadian phase with bright morning light exposure.
problem: Delayed sleep phase tendency, morning grogginess, jet-lag eastward prep support.
typical: 10–30 minutes outdoor light soon after waking
minimum: 5–10 minutes on a bright morning (longer if overcast)
steps: Within ~30–60 minutes of waking, go outdoors without sunglasses if safe (do not stare at sun).
Face general outdoor ambient light; cloudy still helps vs indoor.
Combine with movement if desired.
In evening, dim indoor lights to avoid delaying circadian phase.
For jet lag: timing depends on direction/phase—use careful schedules.
when: Daily circadian anchoring; seasonal low light; mild DSPS tendencies.
short: Increased alertness; morning melatonin suppression supports wake consolidation.
long: Regular morning light helps stabilize circadian timing; clinical chronotherapy uses timed light for circadian rhythm disorders (AASM parameters).
mechanism: Intrinsically photosensitive retinal ganglion cells (melanopsin) signal SCN; morning light advances/stabilizes phase depending on prior phase.
research: Circadian photoreception science; AASM practice parameters for circadian rhythm sleep-wake disorders; jet-lag intervention reviews (Frontiers Physiol 2019).
risks: UV skin/eye risk—use sensible outdoor practice; manic precipitation rare in bipolar with very bright light therapy boxes—medical supervision for clinical light boxes.
avoid: Ocular conditions per ophthalmologist; bipolar—coordinate timed bright light with clinician.
creator: Circadian biology / sleep medicine field.

name: Brief Nap Protocol (10–20 min)
purpose: Reduce sleepiness and restore alertness without deep-sleep inertia.
problem: Afternoon sleepiness, performance dip, partial sleep restriction recovery assist.
steps: Nap early afternoon when possible (circadian nap window).
Set alarm for 10–20 minutes; dark cool place.
Optional caffeine-nap: caffeine immediately before nap so it kicks in on waking (practical; evidence mixed).
Avoid 60–90+ min naps if inertia or night insomnia is a problem.
If chronic insomnia, avoid naps per stimulus control unless clinician allows.
when: Sleep-restricted days, shift workers (with care), students—avoid if it ruins night sleep.
short: Improved alertness and cognitive performance for many after brief naps.
long: Habitual long daytime sleep can fragment nocturnal sleep in insomnia; brief naps are a tool, not a fix for chronic sleep debt.
mechanism: Reduce homeostatic sleep pressure partially; avoid slow-wave heavy sleep that causes inertia.
research: Nap/performance literature in sleep science; operational studies support brief naps. Insomnia guidelines often discourage naps.
risks: Sleep inertia if longer; nocturnal insomnia worsening.
avoid: Chronic insomnia under stimulus control; untreated severe OSA; immediately before high-risk driving if inertia risk.
sources: Sleep research reviews on napping and performance; AASM insomnia guidance on naps.
creator: N/A (operational sleep science practice).

name: Jet Lag Light and Melatonin Timing (Careful Protocol)
purpose: Accelerate circadian adaptation after time-zone travel using timed light and, when appropriate, melatonin.
problem: Jet lag insomnia/sleepiness after east/west flights.
typical: Plan 2–3 days pre-travel + several days post-arrival
minimum: Correct first-day light timing at destination + sleep opportunity alignment
steps: Determine shift direction: eastward generally needs phase advance; westward phase delay.
Seek bright light at times that push clock in desired direction; avoid light at opposing times (use reputable jet-lag planners/clinicians).
Melatonin (when appropriate): often discussed at destination bedtime for eastward travel—individualize; medical advice for dosing.
Hydrate; strategic short naps; avoid alcohol as sleep aid.
Consider pre-shifting sleep 30–60 min/day before departure for large shifts.
when: Flights crossing multiple time zones.
short: Reduced jet-lag severity when timing is correct; wrong timing can worsen misalignment.
long: Faster adaptation over days; melatonin has better evidence for jet lag than many supplements.
mechanism: Light is primary zeitgeber to SCN; melatonin signals biological night and can phase-shift depending on timing.
research: AASM circadian practice parameters; jet-lag reviews (Frontiers Physiol 2019). Melatonin evidence for jet lag stronger than for primary chronic insomnia.
risks: Melatonin next-day drowsiness; light therapy mania risk; incorrect timing.
avoid: Self-prescribe high-dose melatonin in pregnancy, autoimmune disease, or with interacting meds without clinician. Bipolar: caution with bright light.
creator: Chronobiology / sleep medicine field protocols.

name: Fixed Wake-Time Sleep Schedule
purpose: Stabilize circadian and homeostatic systems with consistent wake time.
problem: Social jet lag, irregular sleep timing, weekend oversleep cycles.
typical: Daily habit; wake time within ±30 min
minimum: 7 consecutive days of fixed wake time
steps: Choose a wake time you can keep 7 days/week.
Get morning light soon after waking.
Allow bedtime to flex slightly with sleepiness (especially with stimulus control).
Avoid large weekend phase shifts.
Track for 2 weeks before judging.
when: Irregular schedules; mild insomnia; circadian instability.
short: More predictable sleepiness in evening over days.
long: Foundational chronobiological hygiene; supports CBT-I.
mechanism: Stabilizes circadian phase and sleep pressure patterns.
research: Circadian science; CBT-I stimulus control includes fixed wake time; social jet lag research.
risks: Sleep debt if bedtime too late with early fixed wake—protect sleep opportunity.
avoid: Shift workers need specialized schedules.
creator: Sleep medicine / CBT-I practice.

name: Evening Light Hygiene (Dim and Warm)
purpose: Reduce circadian delay from evening bright/blue-enriched light.
problem: Late sleep onset from screens/overhead LEDs.
steps: Dim overhead lights 2–3 hours before bed; prefer lamps.
Reduce phone/laptop brightness; night mode helps comfort (circadian benefit imperfect).
Avoid bright bathroom lights near bedtime if possible.
Keep bedroom dark for sleep.
when: Delayed sleep phase tendencies; screen-heavy evenings.
short: Easier melatonin rise and sleepiness for many.
long: Supports circadian alignment with morning light.
mechanism: Reduce evening melanopsin stimulation that delays circadian phase and suppresses melatonin.
research: Circadian photoreception and evening light studies; sleep medicine light hygiene guidance.
risks: Unduly fearing all screens; shame cycles—be practical.
avoid: Night-shift workers need different timing strategies.
sources: Circadian lighting research reviews; AASM-related circadian guidance.
creator: Chronobiology field.

name: Acute Physiological Sigh (1–3 Cycles)
purpose: Fastest practical application of cyclic sigh pattern for spike stress.
problem: Panic-adjacent spike, argument aftermath, sudden performance fear.
steps: Stop amplifying the stressor briefly if safe.
Nasal inhale; second short nasal top-up; long exhale (mouth or nose).
Repeat 1–3 times.
Name one next controllable action.
when: In the moment; can be done discreetly.
short: Often noticeable exhale-related relief; not guaranteed panic abort.
long: Same family as cyclic sighing daily practice evidence.
mechanism: Same as cyclic sighing; acute use is extrapolation from daily RCT + known physiological sigh.
research: Balban et al. 2023 primarily studied 5-min daily cyclic sighing; acute 1–3 cycle use is mechanistically related but less directly trial-defined.
risks: Minimal; overuse as avoidance of needed action/problem-solving.
avoid: If breath focus worsens panic—pair with grounding instead.
creator: See cyclic sighing entry.

name: 5-4-3-2-1 Sensory Grounding
purpose: Interrupt anxiety spiral by orienting attention to present sensory details.
problem: Acute anxiety, dissociation risk, racing thoughts.
steps: Name 5 things you can see.
Name 4 things you can feel/touch.
Name 3 things you can hear.
Name 2 things you can smell (or like the smell of).
Name 1 thing you can taste (or like the taste of).
Optionally add slow exhales between items.
when: Acute anxiety, panic onset, overwhelm, trauma-triggered present-moment need.
short: Often reduced subjective intensity via attentional shift.
long: Skill becomes faster with practice; direct RCT evidence for this exact mnemonic is limited—grounding widely used clinically.
mechanism: Competing attentional resource allocation away from threat imagery; sensory reorientation; DBT/trauma-informed grounding family.
research: Widely taught in clinical practice. Specific 5-4-3-2-1 RCTs sparse; small student studies exist. Practical coping—not strong experimental grade.
risks: Can feel trivializing if used dismissively; smell/taste steps hard in some environments.
avoid: If it becomes compulsive counting ritual in OCD—use clinician-guided alternatives.
sources: Clinical psychoeducation (major medical centers); trauma-informed care curricula.
creator: Exact mnemonic authorship unclear; sensory grounding long used in trauma/anxiety treatment.

name: Brief PMR (Hands-Shoulders-Face)
purpose: Rapid somatic release when full PMR is impractical.
problem: Acute muscle bracing with stress.
steps: Tense fists 5 sec, release 20 sec.
Shrug shoulders to ears 5 sec, release.
Gently tense face/jaw 5 sec, release (avoid TMJ pain).
Take one long exhale; notice warmth/heaviness.
when: At desk, before calls, after startling stress.
short: Local tension reduction.
long: Gateway skill to full PMR.
mechanism: Same as PMR contrast effect.
research: Extrapolated from PMR evidence base (abbreviated PMR commonly used).
risks: Over-tensing injured areas.
avoid: Acute injury to involved muscles.
creator: Derived from Jacobson PMR.

name: Moderate Aerobic Exercise Bout
purpose: Reduce stress/anxiety/depressive symptoms via planned aerobic activity.
problem: Chronic stress, low mood, anxiety symptoms, sedentary load.
minimum: 10–15 minutes brisk movement if that is all available
steps: Choose sustainable modality (brisk walk, cycle, swim, jog).
Warm up 3–5 min.
Work at moderate intensity (can talk but not sing) 20–40 min.
Cool down; hydrate.
Aim most days/week for chronic benefits; even single bouts help acute mood for many.
when: Chronic stress management; acute mood lift; foundational health behavior.
short: Often improved mood/anxiety within minutes to hours post-exercise.
long: Meta-analyses support exercise for depressive symptoms; anxiety benefits present but sometimes smaller/less consistent vs active controls.
mechanism: Multiple: monoamines, neurotrophic factors (e.g., BDNF hypotheses), HPA modulation, thermogenic, self-efficacy, sleep improvement.
research: Cochrane exercise for depression reviews; newer umbrella/meta-analyses of exercise for depression/anxiety. Adjunct, not always monotherapy for major clinical disorders.
risks: Injury; cardiac events in high-risk unscreened individuals; overtraining.
avoid: Medical clearance if cardiovascular risk, acute injury, eating-disorder exercise compulsion.
sources: Cochrane Library exercise-depression reviews; recent exercise–anxiety/depression meta-analyses.
creator: N/A (exercise physiology / psychiatry evidence synthesis).

name: Scheduled Worry / Postpone Worry
purpose: Contain rumination by postponing worry to a limited daily worry period.
problem: Uncontrollable worry, bedtime rumination, productivity-killing loops.
typical: 10–20 minute daily worry slot + brief postponement cues
steps: When worry arises outside the slot, jot a brief cue word and postpone: I will worry at 5:30.
Return attention to present task (use grounding if needed).
At the scheduled slot, worry deliberately for 10–20 minutes; problem-solve what is solvable; write unresolved items.
End slot with a transition ritual (walk, wash hands, breathing).
If worry returns after slot, postpone again to tomorrow's slot.
when: GAD-like worry patterns; bedtime mind-racing (combine with stimulus control).
short: Reduced intrusion frequency for many with practice.
long: Component of CBT for worry/GAD; evidence for worry-time techniques within broader CBT packages.
mechanism: Stimulus control for worry; reduces negative reinforcement of continuous worrying; trains attentional control.
research: CBT for GAD literature; Borkovec and related stimulus-control approaches to worry; clinical CBT protocols.
risks: Avoidance of necessary problem-solving if slot is never used for action planning.
avoid: Active crisis/safety issues—do not postpone safety planning. Severe OCD may need ERP specialist approaches.
sources: CBT worry literature; clinical GAD treatment manuals.
creator: Associated with CBT worry treatments (e.g., Borkovec traditions).

name: Mindfulness of Breath (Formal Sitting)
purpose: Train nonjudgmental attention by returning to breath sensations.
problem: Rumination, stress reactivity, attentional instability.
steps: Sit upright; eyes closed or soft gaze.
Feel breath at nostrils, chest, or abdomen.
When mind wanders, note briefly and return—no blame.
Optionally label thinking/feeling then return.
End by widening awareness to room.
when: Daily mind training; stress reduction programs.
short: Occasional calm; often also restlessness (normal).
long: MBSR/MBCT packages show benefits for stress, recurrent depression prevention (MBCT), anxiety symptoms—effects moderate; depend on fidelity.
mechanism: Attention regulation, body awareness, emotion regulation, change in self-perspective (proposed mindfulness mechanisms).
research: MBSR evidence base; MBCT for recurrent depression; Balban 2023 used mindfulness as active comparator (breathwork edged mood/RR).
risks: Trauma reactivation; meditation-related adverse effects in a minority (anxiety, dissociation).
avoid: Active unstable PTSD without trauma-sensitive mindfulness; acute psychosis.
sources: MBSR/MBCT clinical trial literature; meditation adverse effects reviews.
creator: Jon Kabat-Zinn (MBSR); MBCT: Segal, Williams, Teasdale.

name: Micro Social Connection Check-In
purpose: Counter stress isolation with a brief high-quality social contact.
problem: Loneliness-amplified stress; co-rumination risk if misused.
steps: Identify a safe person.
Share specifically (feeling + need) or offer support.
Prefer voice/face when possible.
Avoid co-rumination spirals—balance venting with values/action.
when: After acute stress; low mood isolation.
short: Often affiliative calm and perspective.
long: Social support is among the most robust stress buffers epidemiologically; micro-protocol operationalizes it.
mechanism: Perceived social support modulates stress appraisals and HPA responses.
research: Social support and health psychology literature; loneliness intervention research (heterogeneous).
risks: Venting-only loops; contacting unsafe people.
avoid: Abuse dynamics—use professional/safe channels.
creator: Applied synthesis from social support science.

name: Pre-Performance Routine (PPR)
purpose: Stabilize attention and arousal before a skilled performance via a consistent short sequence.
problem: Choking under pressure, variable warm-up, distracted start.
steps: Define 3–5 steps you can repeat identically (e.g., breath → cue word → visual target → physical set).
Include one arousal tool (e.g., physiological sigh or box breath) and one attentional cue (external focus preferred for many motor skills).
Practice the routine in low-stakes settings until automatic.
Use the same routine in competition/high stakes.
Evaluate and simplify if it becomes over-controlling.
when: Sports, music, presentations, procedural skills, exams.
short: Reduced performance variability; better attentional set.
long: Sport psychology research supports PPRs for consistency under pressure.
mechanism: Attentional control; reduced irrelevant cognitions; arousal regulation; motor preparation consistency.
research: Sport psychology reviews on pre-performance routines; experimental studies under pressure. Effects vary by sport/skill and routine quality.
risks: Superstition/compulsion if overly rigid; time-wasting complexity.
avoid: If routine morphs into OCD-like compulsion—simplify with sport psychologist.
sources: Applied sport psychology literature on routines under pressure.
creator: Applied sport psychology field practice.

name: Centering (Ravizza-Style)
purpose: Rapidly shift from distracted/tense state to controlled, present, process-focused state.
problem: Pre-competition nerves, emotional carryover, loss of composure.
steps: Recognize tension/distraction (awareness).
Pick a physical focal point (e.g., podium edge).
Diaphragmatic breath; release shoulders/jaw on exhale.
Use a short process cue (see seams, smooth start) not outcome (win).
Commit to first action.
when: Between plays, backstage, before a critical attempt.
short: Regain composure and external/process focus.
long: Part of mental skills packages; limited standalone RCTs for branded sequence—supported within broader arousal/attention control evidence.
mechanism: Breath + attentional narrowing to controllable process cues; interrupt threat-oriented self-talk.
research: Ken Ravizza applied sport psychology teachings; empirical support largely from related PPR/breath/attention research.
risks: Over-centering delaying action; inward focus harming automatic skills if too internal.
avoid: Prefer external focus cues for many closed motor skills.
sources: Ravizza applied materials; sport psychology centering descriptions.
creator: Ken Ravizza (popularized centering in sport psychology).

name: PETTLEP Imagery
purpose: Mentally rehearse performance with functional equivalence to real execution.
problem: Skill learning limits, travel without practice access, confidence/preparation gaps.
steps: Physical: imagery in similar stance/clothing when possible.
Environment: include venue details (or photos/video).
Task: image the exact skill/tactics.
Timing: real-time speed (not slow-mo unless drilling a cue).
Learning: update imagery as skill level changes.
Emotion: include typical competition emotions at manageable intensity.
Perspective: usually prefer first-person for motor skills; experiment.
Pair with physical practice when possible; imagery supplements, rarely replaces, practice.
when: Skill acquisition, return-from-injury adjunct, pre-competition activation.
short: Improved readiness and cue familiarity.
long: Systematic reviews support PETTLEP-informed imagery for sport performance, especially with physical practice.
mechanism: Functional equivalence / overlapping motor cognitive networks; motivational and cognitive rehearsal.
research: Holmes & Collins 2001 PETTLEP model; 2022 systematic reviews on PETTLEP and sport performance.
risks: Anxiety amplification if imagery is catastrophe-focused; neglecting physical training.
avoid: Active psychosis with imagery conflation; severe PTSD without guidance if imagery triggers trauma.
creator: Paul Holmes & Dave Collins (PETTLEP model).

name: Implementation Intentions (If–Then Plans)
purpose: Link situational cues to goal-directed responses to automate follow-through.
problem: Intention–behavior gap, forgotten habits, stalled goals.
typical: 5–10 minutes to write plans; seconds to execute
minimum: One precise if–then for one behavior
steps: Specify a critical cue: If situation X occurs…
Specify a concrete response: …then I will do Y (physical, observable).
Make X detectable (time, place, preceding action).
Optionally add obstacle if–thens: If craving hits after lunch, then I walk 5 minutes.
Review plans daily until automatic.
when: Habit formation, health behaviors, study plans, performance cues.
short: Higher likelihood of enacting intended behavior when cue appears.
long: Meta-analyses show medium effects on goal attainment historically (classic d≈0.65; interpret with heterogeneity/publication-bias caution).
mechanism: Delegates control to situational cues; reduces deliberative load; strengthens cue–response links.
research: Gollwitzer & Sheeran meta-analytic work on implementation intentions; extensive experimental literature.
risks: Overly many plans causing clutter; rigid plans that ignore context—revise.
avoid: Not a therapy for clinical depression amotivation alone—combine with care.
creator: Peter Gollwitzer.

name: Tactical Breath Reset (Short Box-like)
purpose: Short box-like reset emphasizing comfort over long holds for performance.
problem: Pre-performance adrenaline with need to stay sharp (not sleepy).
steps: Inhale 4, hold 2–4 (only if comfortable), exhale 4, hold 2–4.
Keep eyes open on task-relevant target.
End on exhale; execute first action cue.
when: Seconds before performance when cyclic sighing feels too downshifting.
short: Composure with alertness preserved better than long meditation.
long: Practical; evidence inferential from paced breathing + PPR research.
mechanism: Attentional scaffolding + mild autonomic regulation.
research: See box breathing + PPR entries.
risks: Holds too long → dizziness.
avoid: Hold-intolerant individuals—use exhale-only pacing.
sources: Applied tactical breathing education; Balban 2023 box arm.
creator: Tactical/performance popularization; applied synthesis.

name: WOOP (Mental Contrasting + Implementation Intentions)
purpose: Increase goal attainment by contrasting wished future with real obstacles, then forming if–then plans.
problem: Fantasy-only goal setting that fails on contact with reality; motivation without strategy.
steps: Wish: choose a meaningful, challenging, feasible wish.
Outcome: vividly imagine the best outcome and how it would feel.
Obstacle: identify the main inner obstacle (habit, emotion, belief)—be honest.
Plan: form If [obstacle], then I will [action].
Repeat for key goals; revisit weekly.
when: Personal/health/academic/work goals; de-biasing pure positive visualization.
short: Clearer commitment when expectancy is adequate; sometimes decreased commitment if goal is unrealistic (feature, not bug).
long: MCII meta-analyses show small–moderate benefits for goal attainment; useful low-cost strategy.
mechanism: Mental contrasting energizes goal pursuit when expectations are sufficient by linking future to present obstacle; II automates obstacle response (Oettingen + Gollwitzer).
research: Oettingen mental contrasting; WOOP practicalization; Frontiers Psychology 2021 MCII meta-analysis (g≈0.34; trim-and-fill lower). Health behavior MCII meta-analyses similar.
risks: Demotivation if wish is fantasy-only with low expectancy—may correctly reduce pursuit.
avoid: Not for acute suicidality/crisis planning—seek professional care.
creator: Gabriele Oettingen (mental contrasting/WOOP); II with Peter Gollwitzer.

name: SMART Goals with Evidence Caveats
purpose: Structure goals as Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Time-bound—while recognizing SMART is a heuristic, not a magic formula.
problem: Vague goals; also over-constraining exploratory/creative aims.
minimum: Rewrite one vague goal into a testable next action
steps: Write the goal specifically (what/when/where).
Define measurement and a check-in date.
Reality-check achievability with constraints.
Confirm relevance to values (avoid inherited shoulds).
Set time bound and first if–then plan.
Caveat: for learning/creative goals, pair with process metrics, not only outcome KPIs.
when: Project planning, team OKRs translation to personal actions.
short: Clarity and coordination.
long: Organizational practice support; experimental superiority of SMART acronym vs other frameworks is not strongly established as unique—implementation quality matters more.
mechanism: Reduces ambiguity; enables feedback; may increase commitment via concreteness.
research: SMART popular management heuristic (Doran 1981 often cited). Goal-setting theory (Locke & Latham) has stronger evidence for specific difficult goals + feedback than for the SMART acronym per se.
risks: False precision; neglecting autonomy/mastery; demotivating impossible A.
avoid: Using SMART to micromanage recovery from depression—prefer values + tiny actions with clinician/coach.
sources: Locke & Latham goal-setting theory reviews; Doran SMART note.
creator: George T. Doran (SMART popularization); Locke & Latham (goal-setting science).

name: Habit Stacking (Routine-Based Cueing)
purpose: Attach a new tiny behavior to an existing reliable routine cue.
problem: Forgetting new habits; weak cues.
typical: 2–5 minutes to design; seconds to perform
minimum: One stack: After [current habit], I will [new habit <2 min].
steps: Identify a stable daily routine (make coffee, brush teeth).
Attach a tiny version of the new habit immediately after.
Keep the new habit laughably small initially.
Increase only after automaticity grows.
Label: popularized by James Clear; scientifically closest to implementation intentions / habit cue research.
when: Building keystone micro-habits.
short: Higher consistency if cue is truly stable.
long: Habit formation depends heavily on repetition in stable contexts; stack type (routine vs time) may matter less than consistent repetition (RCT evidence).
mechanism: Cue–behavior association; reduces prospective memory load.
research: Popular science (Atomic Habits). Underlying science: implementation intentions; Wood/Neal habit research; RCTs on routine- vs time-based cue planning.
risks: Stacking onto unstable cues; ego inflation from reading without practicing.
avoid: Relying on books alone for clinical behavior change needs.
sources: Habit formation RCTs; Gollwitzer II literature; Clear as popularizer.
creator: Popularized by James Clear; related ideas in behavior analysis and BJ Fogg Tiny Habits.

name: Process Visualization (vs Outcome-Only Fantasy)
purpose: Mentally rehearse steps and obstacle handling—not only the trophy moment.
problem: Motivational fantasy without planning; manifestation confusion.
steps: Visualize the process: starting, mid-friction, completing the key action.
Include realistic obstacles and your coping response.
Avoid only imagining applause/outcome (can reduce effort—mental contrasting literature).
End by writing one if–then for today's obstacle.
Separate layers: (1) psych mechanisms—planning, motivation, arousal; (2) traditional/spiritual meaning-making if personally valued; (3) do NOT treat supernatural causation as scientific.
when: Skill goals, training adherence, interview prep.
short: Increased preparedness and intention clarity.
long: Process imagery and mental contrasting outperform pure positive fantasy for attainment in research programs.
mechanism: Cognitive simulation supports planning and self-efficacy; outcome fantasy alone may satiate motivation (Oettingen).
research: Oettingen mental contrasting vs indulging; sport imagery literature; contrast with unsupported Law of Attraction claims.
risks: Confusing visualization with evidence of future events.
avoid: Presenting supernatural manifestation as science—see Unsupported Claims file.
creator: Synthesis of Oettingen + sport/clinical imagery practices.

name: Values Compass (Brief ACT/Values Clarification)
purpose: Clarify valued directions to guide goals when motivation is chaotic.
problem: Goal conflict, borrowed goals, emptiness after achievement.
minimum: 10 minutes picking top 3 values + one action each
steps: List candidate values (connection, growth, courage, health, creativity, etc.).
Pick 3 that feel chosen (not only imposed).
For each, write one 10-minute action this week that expresses it.
Use values as compass when emotions pull off course.
when: Quarterly reset; career confusion; emotion-driven goal churn.
short: Increased sense of meaning/choice.
long: Values work is central in ACT; evidence mainly at package level.
mechanism: Motivated behavior via chosen meaning; reduces pliance-only goals.
research: ACT values components; meaning/values psychological research.
risks: Intellectual values without action.
avoid: Using values talk to avoid concrete help for clinical depression.
sources: ACT values exercises (Hayes/Wilson); values clarification literature.
creator: ACT community / values clarification traditions.

name: TIPP (DBT Crisis Survival Skill)
purpose: Rapidly change body chemistry to reduce extreme emotional arousal.
problem: Emotional crisis, urge surfing need, acute overwhelm.
minimum: 1 TIPP element for 30–60 seconds (e.g., cold water)
steps: Temperature: cold water on face / cold pack / brief cold shower (dive-reflex informed); caution with heart conditions.
Intense exercise: short burst (e.g., 20–60 sec jumping jacks) if safe.
Paced breathing: slow exhale-emphasized breathing.
Progressive relaxation: paired muscle relaxation.
Use as bridge to later problem-solving—not as only long-term strategy.
when: Emotional intensity 8–10/10; before destructive impulses.
short: Often reduced peak arousal within minutes.
long: DBT skills training packages have evidence for emotion dysregulation populations; isolated TIPP RCTs limited—clinically established within DBT.
mechanism: Cold face stimulation can trigger mammalian dive reflex (parasympathetic); exercise metabolizes arousal; breathing/PMR reduce somatic tension.
research: Linehan DBT manuals; evidence strongest for DBT programs overall, not each micro-skill in isolation. Physiological rationale for cold/dive reflex is plausible.
risks: Cold water + cardiac issues; intense exercise injury; misuse as chronic avoidance of therapy.
avoid: Cardiovascular disease—modify Temperature; eating disorders—careful with exercise; seek emergency care for safety risk.
sources: DBT skills training handouts (Linehan); clinical DBT outcome literature.
creator: Marsha Linehan / DBT skills framework.

name: Opposite Action (DBT Skill — Not Full Therapy)
purpose: Act opposite to emotion-driven urges when emotion is unjustified or unhelpful in intensity/duration.
problem: Emotion-consistent actions that worsen problems (avoid when fear unjustified; isolate when sad).
typical: Minutes to hours depending on action
minimum: One small opposite action in the next 10 minutes
steps: Name the emotion and the urge.
Check the facts: is the emotion justified by evidence? Is intensity matching?
If emotion/urge is not justified or not effective, choose opposite action (e.g., approach when fear unjustified; gentle activity when sadness urges withdrawal).
Do opposite action all the way (posture, expression, thoughts aligned).
This is a skill excerpt—not delivery of full DBT therapy.
when: When emotions drive ineffective behavior and facts do not fully support the urge.
short: Reduced emotion intensity after opposite action for many.
long: Component of DBT emotion regulation; package evidence > isolated skill trials.
mechanism: Breaks emotion–action feedback loops; behavioral exposure-like effects when approaching avoided cues.
research: DBT skills manuals; emotion regulation research on behavioral opposite strategies.
risks: Opposite action can be wrong if emotion is justified (e.g., fear of real danger)—always check facts first.
avoid: Safety threats, abuse situations, or medical danger—do not opposite-action away from real risk.
creator: Marsha Linehan (DBT).

name: Cognitive Reappraisal
purpose: Change emotional impact by changing interpretation of a situation.
problem: Catastrophic appraisals, anger/anxiety amplification via meaning-making.
steps: Identify the situation and automatic appraisal (This means I am doomed).
Generate alternative appraisals that are realistic (not toxic positivity).
Ask: evidence for/against? Other explanations? What would I tell a friend?
Choose a balanced reappraisal and note how body emotion shifts.
If stuck in deep belief structures, use full CBT with a clinician.
when: Anxiety/anger spikes driven by interpretation; post-event processing.
short: Reduced negative emotion intensity when reappraisal succeeds.
long: Core CBT/emotion regulation strategy with substantial laboratory and clinical support (Gross process model; CBT trials).
mechanism: Prefrontal modulation of limbic responses via meaning change (proposed); reduces secondary elaborative processing.
research: James Gross emotion regulation framework; CBT outcome literature; experimental reappraisal studies.
risks: Intellectualization avoiding needed action; invalidating real injustice with forced reappraisal.
avoid: Acute trauma processing needs specialized care; psychosis—reality testing with professionals.
sources: Gross emotion regulation reviews; CBT clinical guidelines.
creator: Formalized in emotion regulation science by James Gross; clinical roots in CBT (Beck et al.).

name: Affect Labeling (Putting Feelings into Words)
purpose: Reduce emotional reactivity by specifically naming felt emotions.
problem: Diffuse distress, amygdala-driven reactivity, alexithymic vagueness.
minimum: One precise label (I feel angry and ashamed)
steps: Pause; notice body cues.
Choose specific emotion words (not just bad/fine).
Say or write: I am noticing anxiety/sadness/anger…
Optionally rate intensity 0–10.
Then choose a follow-up skill (breath, reappraisal, opposite action) if needed.
when: Rising emotion; conflict; journaling; panic early signs.
short: Often dampened limbic reactivity; subjective relief varies.
long: Supports emotional granularity associated with better regulation in observational/experimental work.
mechanism: Lieberman et al.: affect labeling increases right vlPFC activity and reduces amygdala responses—implicit emotion regulation.
research: Lieberman et al. 2007 Psychological Science Putting Feelings Into Words (PubMed 17576282); Torre & Lieberman reviews on affect labeling.
risks: In some high-reactivity contexts labeling alone may be insufficient or inconsistently helpful.
avoid: Not a standalone treatment for PTSD/clinical depression.
creator: Research program associated with Matthew Lieberman and colleagues.

name: Cold Face Stimulation (Dive-Reflex Informed)
purpose: Acutely increase parasympathetic tone via cold stimulus to face.
problem: Peak emotional arousal, anger/panic spike (TIPP Temperature element).
steps: Bend forward; apply cold water or cold pack to face especially forehead/eyes/cheeks.
Or hold breath briefly while face in cold water bowl (only if safe/healthy).
Breathe slowly after.
Stop if pain or cardiac symptoms.
when: Emotional crisis skill; not a required daily biohack.
short: Heart rate often drops; subjective intensity may fall.
long: Useful crisis tool within DBT; not a chronic anxiety cure.
mechanism: Trigeminal/cold-triggered mammalian dive reflex → vagal bradycardia.
research: Dive reflex physiology; DBT TIPP rationale. Clinical skill evidence mostly package-level.
risks: Arrhythmia risk in susceptible; cold shock; unsafe if epilepsy/heart disease.
avoid: Cardiac disease, eating disorders with cold purging patterns, unsupervised breath-hold in water.
sources: DBT TIPP; dive reflex physiology references.
creator: DBT TIPP Temperature skill; dive reflex science older.

name: Brief Gratitude Listing
purpose: Shift attention toward valued positives without denying problems.
problem: Negativity bias load, mild low mood, relationship taking-for-granted.
steps: Write 3 specific things you are grateful for today (details beat generics).
Include why it mattered or who helped.
Optionally share one with a person (gratitude expression).
Do not use to gaslight yourself out of real problems.
when: Mild low mood, relationship maintenance, journaling.
short: Small mood bump for some.
long: Positive psychology interventions show small average wellbeing effects; heterogeneity high; not depression monotherapy.
mechanism: Attentional deployment toward positives; social bonding when expressed.
research: Emmons & McCullough gratitude experiments; positive psychology meta-analyses (small effects).
risks: Spiritual bypassing; shame if forced during grief.
avoid: Acute grief/trauma—permission to not be grateful; clinical depression needs proper care.
creator: Research popularized by Robert Emmons & Michael McCullough.

name: Self-Distancing Reflection
purpose: Reduce emotional entanglement by reflecting in third person or fly-on-wall perspective.
problem: Immersive rumination about interpersonal stress.
steps: Recall a stressful social event briefly.
Rewrite or silently narrate using your name / third person or observer perspective.
Ask what advice you would give from that distance.
Extract one learning + one next behavior.
when: Post-conflict processing; journal rumination interrupt.
short: Lower emotional reactivity; more constructive insight often.
long: Experimental work (Kross & Ayduk) supports self-distancing for adaptive reflection.
mechanism: Psychological distance reduces immersion; enables reconstrual.
research: Kross & Ayduk self-distancing research program.
risks: Avoidance if used to never feel emotions; intellectualization.
avoid: Processing severe trauma alone—use therapist.
creator: Ethan Kross, Ozlem Ayduk and colleagues.

name: Cognitive Defusion (Brief ACT Skill)
purpose: Reduce literal believability of thoughts by seeing them as mental events.
problem: Fusion with unhelpful thoughts (I am a failure experienced as fact).
minimum: 30–60 seconds (I am having the thought that…)
steps: Notice the sticky thought.
Preface: I am having the thought that… or sing the thought silly / imagine it on leaves.
Return to valued action while thought may still be present.
This is a skill excerpt—not full ACT therapy delivery.
when: Rumination, perfectionism thoughts, anxiety cognitions.
short: Less struggle with thoughts; more wiggle room to act.
long: ACT packages have evidence for various problems; micro-defusion exercises are components.
mechanism: Changes relationship to cognition rather than content; reduces experiential avoidance.
research: ACT RCTs/meta-analyses for package; defusion experimental tasks in ACT literature (Hayes et al.).
risks: Invalidating need for cognitive restructuring when thoughts are distorted and restructuring helps.
avoid: Acute psychosis; use clinician-guided ACT for clinical disorders.
sources: Hayes ACT literature; Twohig/Levin ACT reviews.
creator: Steven C. Hayes and ACT co-developers.

name: Brief Attention Restoration (Soft Fascination Break)
purpose: Restore directed attention fatigue via brief soft-fascination environments.
problem: Mental fatigue after prolonged focus, irritability, error-proneness.
minimum: 5 minutes looking at nature / window greenery / sky
steps: Stop effortful work.
Expose yourself to a restorative setting: trees, sky, aquarium, nature video if outdoor impossible.
Allow soft fascination—gentle interest without hard focus.
Avoid filling the break with email/social feeds (those demand directed attention).
Return to task with one defined next step.
when: Ultradian dips, after deep work blocks, exam study breaks.
short: Subjective refreshed attention; some studies show executive attention benefits after nature exposure.
long: Attention Restoration Theory (Kaplan) supported by mixed but promising evidence; effect sizes and mechanisms debated.
mechanism: ART: being away, extent, soft fascination, compatibility allow recovery of directed attention capacity.
research: Kaplan ART; nature exposure cognitive studies (heterogeneous).
risks: Breaks that become avoidance; urban access barriers.
avoid: Using as only treatment for ADHD clinical impairment—seek evidence-based ADHD care.
sources: Kaplan Attention Restoration Theory literature; environmental psychology reviews.
creator: Rachel & Stephen Kaplan (Attention Restoration Theory).

name: Task-Switching Buffer
purpose: Reduce switch costs by inserting a brief closure/setup ritual between tasks.
problem: Multitasking residue, errors after abrupt context switches.
steps: Write a one-line parked note: next action for the old task.
Close unrelated tabs/notifications for the new task.
Take 3 slow breaths or one physiological sigh.
State the new task goal in one sentence.
Start with a 2-minute ignition action.
when: Knowledge work, meetings back-to-back, parenting/work switches.
short: Less cognitive residue; cleaner attentional set.
long: Aligned with task-switching cost research—buffers are practical applications rather than a branded evidence-based therapy.
mechanism: Reduces attention residue (Leroy); prepares goal representation for new task.
research: Cognitive psychology of task switching; Sophie Leroy attention residue research. Buffer ritual is applied synthesis.
risks: Over-ritualizing; procrastination disguised as buffering.
avoid: Emergency contexts requiring instant switch.
creator: Applied synthesis from cognitive psychology findings.

name: Tiny Behavioral Activation Step
purpose: Counter rumination/withdrawal by scheduling valued activity in small doses.
problem: Depressive inactivity loops, rumination, anhedonia spirals.
minimum: 2 minutes of the smallest valued action
steps: Pick a valued domain (connection, mastery, service, body).
Define a 2–10 minute action (walk to mailbox, text a friend, wash one dish).
Schedule it; do it regardless of motivation (action first).
Note mood 0–10 before/after without judgment.
Build upward; for clinical depression use full BA with clinician.
when: Low mood, rumination, stuckness; as CBT/BA skill excerpt.
short: Often small mood lift; interrupts brooding.
long: Behavioral activation has strong evidence for depression as a therapy package.
mechanism: Increases response-contingent positive reinforcement; breaks avoidance–rumination cycles.
research: Behavioral activation RCTs and meta-analyses for depression; BA as efficacious psychotherapy.
risks: Pushing manic overactivity; ignoring medical fatigue causes.
avoid: If suicidal or severe depression—urgent professional care. Bipolar: structure with clinician.
sources: BA clinical trial literature; CBT/BA treatment guidelines.
creator: Behavioral activation traditions (e.g., Martell, Dimidjian, Jacobson lineages).

name: Focused Work Block + Break (Pomodoro-style)
purpose: Protect deep focus with time-boxed work and deliberate recovery breaks.
problem: Distractibility, burnout from unbroken screen time.
steps: Choose one task; set timer (25 or personalized).
Work until timer; park distractions on a notepad.
Break: stand, eyes off near screens, brief walk/breath—no new rabbit holes.
After 3–4 cycles, take a longer break (15–30 min).
Adjust lengths to your ultradian rhythm.
when: Knowledge work, studying, creative execution.
short: Improved subjective focus and completion cadence.
long: Popular productivity method; empirical literature mixed/limited vs strong marketing—useful as structure, not magic.
mechanism: Reduces decision fatigue; creates implementation cue from timer; breaks restore attention.
research: Limited rigorous trials of classic Pomodoro; related evidence from break/attention and timeboxing practices.
risks: Timer anxiety; interrupting flow states inappropriately—flex when in deep flow.
avoid: Tasks needing long uninterrupted immersion—use longer blocks.
sources: Francesco Cirillo Pomodoro Technique materials; attention/break research adjacency.
creator: Francesco Cirillo (Pomodoro Technique).
